title: Google Review Card Staff Prompt Playbook
summary: A staff-prompt playbook for Google review cards that makes the ask feel like part of service — covering timing, wording, handoff motion, training rhythm, decay prevention and a four-week pilot that tests staff behaviour before printing a large branded batch.
heroPoints: The best staff prompt feels like part of service — not a corporate add-on script staff tolerate for six weeks and then drop.
Different teams can sustain different levels of prompt: a hand-delivered card, a quick point to a stand, or a purely self-serve placement.
Rollout works better when managers test staff behaviour for four weeks before printing branded cards at scale.

sections.title: Why the prompt matters more than the script
sections.intro: Operators tend to obsess about the wording of the ask. The wording matters, but the timing and motion of the prompt matter more. A clumsy script at the right moment outperforms a perfect script at the wrong moment.
bullets: Customers decide whether to engage with a review prompt in the first two seconds. That window is controlled by when staff asks, not by the specific words used.
A natural prompt at the right moment produces 5–15% conversion. An awkward prompt at the wrong moment produces under 1%, regardless of how polished the script reads.
The prompt has to fit the service rhythm. If asking for a review interrupts the handoff flow, staff drops the script within days; if it completes the handoff flow, staff sustains it for months.

sections.title: Finding the right service moment
sections.intro: Every hospitality and service workflow has a natural pause point. The prompt belongs inside that pause — not before it, not after it.
bullets: Restaurants: after settling the bill, before the card machine leaves the table. The customer is about to leave anyway; the prompt adds seconds, not friction.
Retail: after the payment terminal confirms and the receipt prints. The customer is waiting for the card to return; the prompt fills that wait.
Hotels: at checkout, after the folio is settled and the key card is collected. The customer is about to depart; a short card handoff slots neatly in.
Salons and spas: at the front desk after the service is complete and payment is done. The customer is in a post-service glow; the prompt captures that mood.
Pickup counters: while the order is being bagged. Twenty seconds of attention the customer is already giving the counter.

Wrong moment indicators: before service is complete (the review isn't earned), during payment (the customer is distracted), when a queue is waiting (staff feels rushed), when there is any sign of dissatisfaction (the prompt feels tone-deaf).

sections.title: Scripts that survive three weeks of service pressure
sections.intro: A script has to be short enough to use under pressure and flexible enough to sound different coming from different staff members. Corporate-tone scripts fail; conversational scripts survive.
bullets: Base ask: 'If you had a good time with us, a quick Google review helps us a lot.' Handed card. That's the entire prompt.
Add warmth: 'Hope you enjoyed dinner — a Google review would mean the world to our chef.' The emotional hook belongs in the second sentence, not the first.
Hotel variant: 'Thanks for staying with us. If your visit was good, a quick Google review helps the next guest find us.'
Retail variant: 'Glad we could help find what you were looking for. If you have 30 seconds for a Google review, it really helps the shop.'
Avoid corporate phrasing: 'We would appreciate your feedback on our Google Business Profile' sounds like a survey, not a chat. Customers disengage.
Never sound conditional: 'If you wouldn't mind...' and 'only if you have time...' signal that the ask is unimportant. The ask has to feel confident to convert.

sections.title: The handoff motion
sections.intro: The physical motion of handing over the card is as important as the script. Practised well, the motion takes three seconds and feels like service; practised badly, it feels like upselling.
bullets: Card is already in the staff's hand before the prompt starts. Reaching for a card while saying the script halves the conversion.
Card is placed on the counter face up or handed over with a specific gesture (a small two-finger offer, not a thrust). The card should feel offered, not imposed.
Eye contact at the moment of handover. A card handed over while looking at the till reads as afterthought.
Slight smile on delivery. The prompt should feel like warmth, not a sales request.
Walk-away: staff immediately returns to service or moves on. Hovering for the customer to tap creates pressure and reduces conversion.
For stand-based placements, the motion is a point and a sentence: 'there's a quick Google review card here if you have 30 seconds'. The customer decides the pace.

sections.title: Training rhythm and decay prevention
sections.intro: Staff prompts decay within four to six weeks unless actively maintained. Managers who expect the script to self-sustain are disappointed; managers who build a light training rhythm see sustained results.
bullets: Week 1: training. Five-minute team huddle covering the prompt, the timing, the handoff motion. One role-play per staff member.
Week 2: observation. Manager watches two to three real handoffs per staff member and coaches quietly. No public corrections.
Week 4: first conversion check. Pull Google review velocity. Share the number with the team — 'we went from 5 reviews last month to 18 this month, nice work'.
Week 8: refresh. One team huddle revisiting the prompt. Address any drift, celebrate high performers.
Month 3+: monthly review velocity check. If conversion drops 20%+, diagnose whether it's prompt decay, staff churn, or a placement issue.
New-hire onboarding: the prompt is part of the service training from day one, not an optional add-on.
Managerial signal: if managers do not prompt themselves on the floor, staff correctly reads it as low priority and the programme dies.

sections.title: Matching prompt style to team reality
sections.intro: Not every team can sustain a hand-delivered prompt. Forcing one on a team that cannot support it produces worse results than designing around the team's real capacity.
bullets: High-touch teams (fine dining, luxury hotels, premium salons): hand-delivered card with a personalised ask. Conversion is high and feels on-brand.
Mid-touch teams (casual restaurants, hotel front desks at scale, mid-tier retail): card handoff with a short general script. Conversion is solid with moderate training investment.

High-volume teams (fast casual, convenience retail, pickup counters): gesture to a stand or sticker, short verbal cue ('quick Google review over there?'). Lower conversion per interaction but high absolute volume.
Low-staff moments (self-service, unattended pickup, delivery drops): no prompt; rely on fixed placement with strong copy.
Franchise teams with high turnover: simpler script, more reliance on physical placement, monthly training refresh built into the shift schedule.

sections.title: A four-week staff-prompt pilot
sections.intro: Before committing to a full print run and a company-wide script, run a structured pilot. Four weeks is the minimum length to see past weekly noise.
bullets: Week 0 — preparation: select one location, pick two to three staff champions, brief them on script and motion. Print 200 pilot cards.
Week 1: observe. Track how often the prompt actually happens. Manager shadows two shifts and counts prompts per 100 transactions.
Week 2: measure. Track Google review velocity against the prior four weeks. Note which staff members prompt most often and which hesitate.
Week 3: coach. Address hesitation individually; share early wins publicly. Adjust the script wording if a specific phrase is consistently hard to deliver.
Week 4: decide. Review velocity lift, staff adoption, customer reaction. Decide whether to scale, iterate, or shift to a self-serve placement.

Pilot exit criteria written before week 0: at least 50% of prompt-eligible transactions see the prompt; review velocity lifts at least 2× over baseline; no staff member actively resists the programme.
Failure modes: if staff will not prompt, redesign as self-serve. If staff prompt but customers do not engage, the moment or the card is wrong. Each failure points to a specific fix.

faq.question: Should every review-card rollout rely on a staff prompt?
faq.answer: No. Some environments benefit from a light self-serve prompt — pickup counters, unattended in-room surfaces, delivery inserts — while others convert far better when staff introduces the card during an existing service handoff. The right answer depends on the team's capacity to sustain a prompt for months, not weeks.

faq.question: What should a staff-prompt pilot measure first?
faq.answer: Whether staff actually uses the prompt at all. Measure prompts-per-100-transactions before measuring review velocity, because review velocity is meaningless if the prompt does not happen. If staff is prompting at least 50% of eligible transactions, then review velocity becomes the signal.

faq.question: What is the right moment to deliver the prompt?
faq.answer: Inside the natural pause at the end of service — after the bill is settled, after the payment terminal confirms, after the room folio is closed. Never during payment (the customer is distracted), never before service completes (the review has not been earned), and never when a queue is visibly waiting (staff feels rushed and delivers a poor prompt).

faq.question: How long should a script be?
faq.answer: One sentence, ideally under 15 words. 'If you had a good time, a quick Google review helps us a lot.' Longer scripts get shortened by staff under service pressure, so the operator loses control of what is actually said. A short script that everyone delivers consistently beats a polished script that drifts.

faq.question: How do you prevent prompt decay?
faq.answer: Light training rhythm. Month 1 training, month 2 refresh, monthly review velocity check from month 3 onward. Share the numbers with the team — a visible lift keeps motivation up. If managers stop prompting themselves on the floor, staff correctly reads the signal and the programme dies within weeks.

faq.question: Can a high-turnover team sustain a staff prompt?
faq.answer: Yes, with adaptations. Shorter script, more reliance on physical placement, monthly training refresh built into shift schedules, and written prompt guidance in the new-hire onboarding packet from day one. The programme will run lower per-interaction conversion than a low-turnover team, but absolute review volume can still be strong with enough transactions.

faq.question: What is the single biggest avoidable mistake in staff prompting?
faq.answer: Writing a long corporate script that no one can realistically use during service. Scripts drift or disappear within weeks; the prompt decays; the programme fails. Start with a short, conversational one-line ask that a stressed staff member can deliver authentically, and iterate from there based on what the team actually says in real handoffs.
